stem: After a customer's account is approved for options trading, within how many days must the firm obtain the customer's signed options agreement?
spoken_stem: After an options account is approved, within how many days must the firm get the customer's signed options agreement?
explanation: Under FINRA Rule 2360, the customer's written agreement to abide by options position and exercise limits and the rules must be obtained within 15 days after the account is approved for options trading. If it is not received, the customer may only close existing positions. The other periods are incorrect.
spoken_explanation: Options account sequence: deliver the disclosure document, a principal approves, and the customer returns the signed agreement within fifteen days. Miss it, and the customer can only close positions. The principal must approve the account before the first trade, using the customer's financial info, experience, and objectives.
outline_ref: 2.4 Required review, approvals and documentation for account opening; 2.1 options accounts

stem: The Options Disclosure Document (ODD) must be delivered to a new options customer:

choices.text: At or before the time the account is approved for options trading
Before the first trade, which may be after approval
Within 15 days after the account is approved
With the confirmation of the first options trade

spoken_stem: When must the Options Disclosure Document be delivered to a new options customer?
explanation: The ODD, 'Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options', must be furnished at or before the time the account is approved for options trading. 15 days after approval is the deadline for the signed options agreement, not the ODD. 'Before the first trade' and 'with the first confirmation' are both too late.
spoken_explanation: The risk disclosure comes first: at or before the account is approved. The fifteen-day window is for the signed agreement, not the disclosure document. Updated disclosure documents must also be sent when the document is revised. Customers sign the options agreement only after receiving the disclosure document.
outline_ref: 2.1 Disclosures regarding account types; 1.1 options disclosure document

stem: Which customer instruction requires prior written discretionary authorization?

choices.text: Buy 300 shares of XYZ today at a price you think is best
Sell some of my XYZ shares today
Buy 100 shares of XYZ at the market
Buy 200 shares of XYZ at 50, good till canceled

spoken_stem: Which instruction needs prior written discretionary authority? A, buy three hundred XYZ today at the best price you think. B, sell some of my XYZ today. C, buy a hundred XYZ at market. D, buy two hundred XYZ at fifty, good till canceled.
explanation: Discretion exists when the RR chooses the asset, the action (buy or sell), or the amount. 'Sell some' leaves the AMOUNT to the RR, so written authorization is required. Choosing only the time and price (choice A) is not discretion, though it is generally limited to the day it is granted. Market and limit orders with asset, action, and amount specified need no discretion.
spoken_explanation: Remember three A's: asset, action, amount. If the rep picks any of them, that's discretion and needs written authority first. Sell some leaves the amount to the rep. Time and price alone isn't discretion. Each discretionary order must be marked discretionary and reviewed by a principal promptly, and the account must be reviewed periodically for excessive trading.
outline_ref: 2.2 Account authorizations: trading authority, discretionary account documents

stem: Two unrelated customers own an account as tenants in common, 60/40. The 60% owner dies. What happens to that 60% interest?

choices.text: It passes to the surviving owner
It passes to the deceased owner's estate
It is split equally between the estate and the survivor

spoken_stem: Two people own an account as tenants in common, sixty forty. The sixty percent owner dies. Where does that share go?
explanation: In a tenants-in-common account, each owner's fractional interest passes to his or her estate at death, so the 60% goes to the deceased's estate. Passing to the survivor is the right of survivorship in a JTWROS account. The account is not frozen permanently, and there is no equal split.
spoken_explanation: Tenants in common: your share goes to your estate. Joint with right of survivorship: it goes to the surviving owner. TIC can also be unequal, like sixty forty. Unlike TIC, JTWROS owners must have equal interests and the account skips probate for the survivor. Tenants in common interests can also be unequal, like sixty forty.
outline_ref: 2.1 Account registration types (TIC)

stem: A 40-year-old leaves her employer and takes a distribution of her $50,000 401(k) balance paid directly to her, intending to roll it into an IRA. Which is TRUE?

choices.text: The plan must withhold 20%, and she has 60 days to roll over the full amount
No withholding applies if she rolls it over within 60 days
She has 90 days to complete the rollover
The plan must withhold 10% as an early withdrawal penalty

spoken_stem: A forty-year-old takes her fifty thousand dollar 401k as a check made out to her, planning to roll it to an IRA. Which is TRUE?
explanation: An eligible rollover distribution paid to the participant (indirect rollover) is subject to mandatory 20% federal withholding: $10,000 here. She has 60 days to deposit the FULL $50,000 into the IRA, making up the withheld $10,000 from other funds to avoid tax on it. A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover avoids withholding. 90 days is wrong. The 10% penalty is not 'withheld'. It is assessed on amounts not rolled over.
spoken_explanation: Check made out to you from a 401k means twenty percent is withheld up front, here ten thousand. You get sixty days to put the full fifty thousand into the IRA. A direct rollover avoids the withholding altogether. A direct rollover, made trustee to trustee, has no withholding and doesn't count as a sixty-day rollover.

stem: True or false: The original owner of a Roth IRA must begin taking required minimum distributions at age 73.

spoken_explanation: False. Roth IRAs have no RMDs for the original owner. Traditional IRAs start RMDs at seventy-three under current law, scheduled to become seventy-five in the next decade. stem: Regulation Best Interest's general obligation is satisfied by complying with each of the following component obligations EXCEPT:
spoken_stem: Reg BI's general obligation is satisfied by meeting each of these component obligations, EXCEPT which? A, disclosure. B, care. C, conflict of interest. D, ongoing account monitoring.
explanation: Reg BI has four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance. It does NOT impose an ongoing duty to monitor a retail customer's account unless the broker-dealer agrees to provide monitoring. Disclosure, Care, and Conflict of Interest are each components.
spoken_explanation: Reg BI's four parts are disclosure, care, conflict of interest, and compliance. Ongoing monitoring isn't required unless the firm agrees to provide it. Reg BI applies when firms recommend securities or strategies to retail customers, including account type recommendations like rolling over to an IRA.

stem: An RR recommends a series of trades to a retail customer. Each trade, viewed alone, is in the customer's best interest, but the account's turnover and cost-to-equity ratio are very high. Which obligation is MOST likely violated?
spoken_stem: A rep recommends trades that each look fine alone, but account turnover and costs are very high. Which obligation is MOST likely violated?
explanation: The quantitative obligation requires that a SERIES of recommended transactions not be excessive in light of the customer's profile, even if each trade is acceptable in isolation. High turnover and cost-to-equity ratios are classic signs of excessive trading (churning). Reasonable-basis relates to understanding the product. Customer-specific relates to fit for this customer of each recommendation. Disclosure relates to telling the customer material facts.
spoken_explanation: One trade at a time looks fine, but the pattern is too much. That's the quantitative obligation: the series of trades can't be excessive. Turnover and cost-to-equity are the red flags for churning. Reasonable basis means understanding the product. Customer-specific means it fits this customer. Quantitative means the overall pattern isn't excessive.
outline_ref: 2.3 Reasonable-basis, customer-specific and quantitative care obligations

stem: An associated person of one FINRA member wants to open a brokerage account at another member firm. Which is required?

choices.text: Nothing, if it is a cash account
The employing firm's prior written consent
Oral approval from the employing firm's principal

spoken_stem: Someone who works for one FINRA member wants to open an account at another member. What's required?
explanation: FINRA Rule 3210 requires the associated person to obtain the prior written consent of the employing member before opening an account at another firm, and the executing firm must provide duplicate confirmations and statements to the employer upon request. Cash accounts are not exempt. FINRA is not notified. Oral approval is insufficient.
spoken_explanation: Working at one firm and opening an account at another requires the employer's prior written consent. The other firm then sends duplicate statements and confirms to your employer on request. Firms must also be alerted when associated persons trade elsewhere so they can monitor for conflicts and insider trading.
